reference.source: Tintinalli's Emergency Medicine / ACSM guidance on exertional rhabdomyolysis
clinicalPearls: The classic triad is muscle pain, weakness, and dark (tea- or cola-coloured) urine following intense or unaccustomed exertion, though not all three are always present
The diagnosis rests on a markedly elevated serum creatine kinase, typically many times the upper limit of normal
The most serious systemic complication is myoglobinuric acute kidney injury, in which released myoglobin causes pigment nephropathy
Dangerous electrolyte derangements include hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and hypocalcaemia, and hyperkalaemia can precipitate life-threatening arrhythmia
Acute compartment syndrome may develop in affected limbs and, conversely, established compartment syndrome can itself cause rhabdomyolysis

Contributing factors include heat, dehydration, certain drugs and supplements, sickle cell trait, and recurrent episodes should prompt evaluation for an underlying metabolic myopathy or malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
The cornerstone of management is early and aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation to protect the kidneys, alongside correction of electrolyte disturbance and vigilance for compartment syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Exertional rhabdomyolysis occurs when strenuous or unaccustomed muscular activity, often compounded by heat, dehydration, or an underlying metabolic susceptibility, exceeds the energy supply of skeletal muscle and causes myocyte membrane injury. Breakdown of muscle cells releases intracellular contents, including creatine kinase, myoglobin, potassium, and phosphate, into the circulation. Myoglobin filtered by the kidney contributes to acute kidney injury through tubular obstruction, direct tubular toxicity, and renal vasoconstriction, an effect worsened by hypovolaemia. Efflux of potassium and phosphate with sequestration of calcium into damaged muscle produces the characteristic electrolyte pattern, while swelling within fascial compartments can raise pressure enough to cause compartment syndrome and further ischaemic muscle injury.
additionalDifferentials: Inherited metabolic myopathy (e.g. disorders of glycogen or fatty acid metabolism)
Myoglobinuria from drug or toxin exposure
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase, with serial measurement to track the course
Renal function and serum electrolytes including potassium, phosphate, and calcium
Urinalysis showing a positive dipstick for blood without red cells, indicating myoglobinuria
Electrocardiography to detect changes of hyperkalaemia
Assessment of hydration status and, where relevant, core temperature for concurrent heat illness
Compartment pressure measurement if compartment syndrome is suspected, and workup for an underlying myopathy in recurrent cases
redFlags: Reduced urine output or rising creatinine indicating acute kidney injury
Hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic changes threatening arrhythmia
A tense, painful limb with pain on passive stretch suggesting compartment syndrome
Concurrent hyperthermia and altered mental state suggesting exertional heat stroke
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and aggressive fluid resuscitation, most patients recover fully and renal function usually normalises. Prognosis worsens with severe acute kidney injury, delayed treatment, or compartment syndrome, and recurrent episodes suggest an underlying predisposition that alters long-term counselling and return-to-activity advice.
pitfalls: Under-resuscitating with fluids and allowing preventable myoglobinuric acute kidney injury
Interpreting a urine dipstick positive for blood as haematuria when it reflects myoglobinuria
Missing evolving compartment syndrome because pain seems in keeping with muscle soreness
Failing to investigate recurrent episodes for a metabolic myopathy or malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
references: Tintinalli's Emergency Medicine: A Comprehensive Study Guide
American College of Sports Medicine guidance on exertional rhabdomyolysis
management: Early, aggressive intravenous crystalloid fluid resuscitation to maintain urine output and prevent myoglobinuric pigment nephropathy
Serial monitoring of creatine kinase, renal function and electrolytes to track the course
Urgent treatment of hyperkalaemia (calcium, insulin-dextrose) with ECG monitoring for arrhythmia, and management of accompanying hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia
Renal replacement therapy for refractory acute kidney injury or life-threatening electrolyte disturbance
Emergency fasciotomy for acute compartment syndrome in the affected limb
Remove precipitants: stop offending drugs and supplements and cool the patient if there is concurrent heat illness
Evaluate for an underlying metabolic myopathy or malignant hyperthermia susceptibility in recurrent episodes
